characters.name: Halcyon Marks
characters.voice: seeks to engineer empathy through machinery — speaks in measured, technical clauses

characters.name: Ansel Marks
characters.arc: Father — wants to maintain order through silence

characters.name: Iyla Petrov Marks
characters.arc: Mother — wants recognition for her intellect

characters.name: Nikola Tesla
characters.arc: Mentor/Antagonist — wants absolute control over energy

characters.name: Elias Marks
characters.arc: Son — wants paternal approval but feels abandoned

characters.name: Clara Marks
characters.arc: Second Wife — wants companionship without intrusion

plot_points.description: Ansel teaches Halcyon to listen to the "hum" of a piano string to find its fault; Halcyon learns that sound has weight.
Iyla recites a lecture on electromagnetic theory to a room of sleeping children, establishing her belief that knowledge is power despite her gender.
Halcyon apprentices with Tesla; they argue over resonance, with Tesla viewing it as control and Halcyon as communication.
Tesla’s public failure and Halcyon’s silent fix; Halcyon realizes his value lies in the background, not the spotlight.
Halcyon meets Marta in a library; he tries to describe her laugh using acoustic frequencies, confusing her.
Marta’s death from influenza; Halcyon builds the first polygraph not to detect lies, but to record the cessation of her pulse.
The polygraph fails to capture the *quality* of her absence, only the data of her end; Halcyon’s grief is unmeasured.
During WWI, Halcyon designs the "Grief Telegraph"; he hopes it will connect soldiers to families, but it only transmits static and panic.
Elias rejects his father’s inventions as soulless; Halcyon retreats into his work, believing complexity is safety.
Halcyon marries Clara; she tolerates his machines but demands he stop talking about them, creating a new kind of silence.
Elias burns the patents; Halcyon watches the fire, realizing his life’s work has been consumed by the very entropy he tried to defy.
The accidental neural net is discovered by a graduate student; Halcyon denies authorship, protecting his son’s narrative.
Halcyon dictates his final letter, admitting that grief is not a signal to be decoded, but a space to be inhabited.
(resolution, ch14) Halcyon dies alone; the machines continue to tick, but no one listens to them.

voice: Close third-person past tense, formally structured with the analytical precision of a technical manual, yet permeated by a lingering, melancholic irony that exposes the gap between Halcyon’s logical models and his emotional reality.
